claim: Many eukaryotes assemble a ring-shaped actomyosin network that contracts to drive cytokinesis.
source: Many eukaryotes assemble a ring-shaped actomyosin network that contracts to drive cytokinesis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about eukaryotic cell division.

claim: The cytokinetic ring disassembles during contraction through an unknown mechanism.
source: Unlike actomyosin in sarcomeres, which cycles through contraction and relaxation, the cytokinetic ring disassembles during contraction through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: During actomyosin ring contraction in S. japonicus and S. pombe, actin filaments are expelled as micron-scale bundles containing multiple actomyosin ring proteins.
source: Here we find in Schizosaccharomyces japonicus and Schizosaccharomyces pombe that, during actomyosin ring contraction, actin filaments associated with actomyosin rings are expelled as micron-scale bundles containing multiple actomyosin ring proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations shown in the figures.

claim: Expulsion of actin bundles does not require continuous presence of cytoplasm.
source: Using functional isolated actomyosin rings we show that expulsion of actin bundles does not require continuous presence of cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using cell ghosts (isolated rings).

claim: Mechanical compression of actomyosin rings results in expulsion of bundles predominantly at regions of high curvature.
source: Strikingly, mechanical compression of actomyosin rings results in expulsion of bundles predominantly at regions of high curvature.
evidence: This is demonstrated by compression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increased curvature of the ring itself promotes its disassembly.
source: Our work unprecedentedly reveals that the increased curvature of the ring itself promotes its disassembly.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Curvature-induced mechanism may operate in disassembly of other contractile networks.
source: It is likely that such a curvature-induced mechanism may operate in disassembly of other contractile networks.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other systems.

claim: During ring contraction, ring components continuously disassemble while maintaining ring contractility.
source: During ring contraction, ring components continuously disassemble while maintaining ring contractility (Pollard and Wu, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Actomyosin in sarcomeres undergoes contraction and relaxation cycles without disassembly.
source: This is in stark contrast to other actomyosin machineries, particularly the thick and thin filament based sarcomeres in muscle fibers, which undergo contraction and relaxation cycles without disassembly (Murrell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on muscle sarcomeres.

claim: ADF1/Cofilin together with Coronin and WD-repeat protein Aip1 modulate actin turnover by severing actin bundles in many types of actin networks.
source: ADF1/Cofilin together with Coronin and WD-repeat protein Aip1 modulate actin turnover by severing actin bundles in many types of actin networks (Jansen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The involvement of ADF1/Cofilin, Coronin, and Aip1 in actomyosin ring contraction and disassembly is still unclear.
source: However, their involvement in actomyosin ring contraction and disassembly is still unclear (Chen and Pollard, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation indicating uncertainty in the field.

claim: Myosin II may regulate disassembly of actin networks during cytokinesis.
source: The F-actin based molecular motor Myosin II may also regulate disassembly of actin networks during cytokinesis (Guha et al., 2005; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005), presumably by myosin II mediated actin filaments buckling and breakage (Murrell and Gardel, 2012; Reymann et al., 2012; Vogel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The exact mechanism governing disassembly of actomyosin rings and whether and how the ring disassembly is coordinated to ring contraction have remained unknown.
source: The exact mechanism governing disassembly of actomyosin rings and whether and how the ring disassembly is coordinated to ring contraction have remained unknown so far.
evidence: This identifies the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: Large F-actin bundles appear to be connected with the contracting ring in S. japonicus cells expressing LifeAct-GFP.
source: Whilst studying F-actin dynamics in S. japonicus cells expressing LifeAct-GFP, as a marker for all actin structures (Gu et al., 2015; Huang et al., 2012; Riedl et al., 2008), large F-actin bundles appeared to be connected with the contracting ring (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In spheroplasts, actomyosin rings were oriented randomly and slid along the cell membrane during contraction.
source: We imaged actin rings in the axial plane to achieve higher resolution by preparing spheroplasts, in which actomyosin rings were oriented randomly and slid along the cell membrane during contraction, consistent with previous work in S. pombe and in reconstituted giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs) (Mishra et al., 2012; Miyazaki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to prior work.

claim: Actin filaments project outwards from the contracting ring in spheroplasts where the actomyosin ring was positioned close to the imaging plane.
source: In spheroplasts where the actomyosin ring was positioned close to the imaging plane, actin filaments appeared to project outwards from the contracting ring (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Permeabilized spheroplasts retained substantial numbers of actin filaments that remained attached to the ring.
source: Permeabilized spheroplasts retained substantial numbers of actin filaments that remained attached to the ring, indicating that the actin filaments were connected to the contracting ring (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Actin filaments connected to the contracting actomyosin ring are not an artifact of LifeAct-GFP.
source: To ensure that the observed actin filaments were not an artifact of LifeAct-GFP used in these experiments, we fixed and stained wild type cells (that did not express any fusion protein) and wild type cells expressing LifeAct-GFP with Rhodamine-conjugated phalloidin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A). We also fixed and stained permeabilized spheroplasts generated from these two strains with Rhodamine-conjugated phalloidin. In both cases, we were able to detect actin filaments connected to the contracting actomyosin ring (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), ruling out the possibility that the observed filaments were an artifact of the tag used.
evidence: This is supported by control experiments using phalloidin staining.

claim: Rlc1p-GFP (and by extension Myosin II) is part of the actin filaments attached to contracting rings.
source: When fixed cells expressing Rlc1p-GFP were stained with Rhodamine-conjugated phalloidin, actin filaments attached to the ring colocalized with Rlc1p, suggesting that Rlc1p-GFP (and by extension Myosin II) was also part of the actin filaments attached to contracting rings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Actin filaments linked to the contracting actomyosin ring were detected in S. pombe cells and permeabilized spheroplasts.
source: Furthermore, actin filaments linked to the contracting actomyosin ring were detected in S. pombe cells and permeabilized spheroplasts of wild type cells (with no genetic tag) and of wild type cells expressing LifeAct-GFP or Rlc1-GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), establishing that this phenomenon is not unique to S. japonicus cells and spheroplasts.
evidence: This is supported by data from S. pombe shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Actin and myosin II filaments attached to contracting actomyosin rings have been observed by Wollrab and colleagues in S. pombe cells.
source: Actin and myosin II filaments attached to contracting actomyosin rings have been observed by Wollrab and colleagues in S. pombe cells, although the significance of these structures was not investigated in their work (Wollrab et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Actomyosin rings are 77 ± 16 nm wide for ring diameters ranging 500 nm to 2.8 µm.
source: Analysis of actomyosin rings with super resolution microscopy STORM showed it to be 77 ± 16 nm wide for ring diameters ranging 500 nm to 2.8 µm, whilst the ring associated actin filamentous structures were 52 ± 12 nm wide (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; enlarged panel), indicating that these structures contained multiple 7 nm-wide actin filaments arranged in a bundle (Takaine and Mabuchi, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by STORM microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ring-associated actin filamentous structures are 52 ± 12 nm wide.
source: Analysis of actomyosin rings with super resolution microscopy STORM showed it to be 77 ± 16 nm wide for ring diameters ranging 500 nm to 2.8 µm, whilst the ring associated actin filamentous structures were 52 ± 12 nm wide (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; enlarged panel), indicating that these structures contained multiple 7 nm-wide actin filaments arranged in a bundle (Takaine and Mabuchi, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by STORM microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Ring-associated actin structures contain multiple 7 nm-wide actin filaments arranged in a bundle.
source: Analysis of actomyosin rings with super resolution microscopy STORM showed it to be 77 ± 16 nm wide for ring diameters ranging 500 nm to 2.8 µm, whilst the ring associated actin filamentous structures were 52 ± 12 nm wide (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; enlarged panel), indicating that these structures contained multiple 7 nm-wide actin filaments arranged in a bundle (Takaine and Mabuchi, 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the measured width and known actin filament diameter.

claim: Actin bundles appear to emerge from the contracting ring, continue to extend in length and are progressively expelled from the sites of their initial appearances.
source: Time-lapse microscopic analysis of spheroplasts expressing LifeAct-GFP showed that actin bundles appeared to emerge from the contracting ring, continued to extend in length and were progressively expelled from the sites of their initial appearances (Figure 1E; Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1E and Video 1.

claim: Upon the expulsion of actin bundles, the contracting ring sometimes disintegrates at the region of release.
source: Occasionally, upon the expulsion of actin bundles, the contracting ring seemed to disintegrate at the region of release (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Actin bundles are expelled from contracting rings in S. pombe.
source: Similar observations of actin bundles being expelled from contracting rings were also made in S. pombe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from S. pombe shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Actin bundles are expelled during contraction in S. japonicus intact cells expressing LifeAct-GFP.
source: Actin bundles were also expelled during contraction in S. japonicus intact cells expressing LifeAct-GFP in which the GFP intensity was reduced and actin appeared disorganized near the end of cytokinesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: The actin intensity in large rings is higher than in small rings in permeabilized spheroplasts.
source: The actin intensity measured in permeabilized spheroplasts using CF633-phalloidin staining in large rings was higher than in small rings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H; Note that the fluorescence intensity from ring-associated bundles were not considered in this analysis).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The combined actin fluorescence intensity from rings and associated bundles is roughly comparable in large and small rings.
source: However, the combined actin fluorescence intensity from rings and associated bundles was roughly comparable in large and small rings (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I), suggesting that the expulsion of actin bundles from the ring may represent a mechanism for ring disassembly.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Approximately 68% of actin filaments that are lost from the ring during contraction are expelled as bundles.
source: We estimated that ~68% of actin filaments that are lost from the ring during contraction (from diameters of 3.48 ± 1.44 µm to 1.23 ± 0.65 µm) are expelled as bundles.
evidence: This is based on quantification of fluorescence intensity shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Rlc1p, Cdc8p, Rng2p, and Cdc15p are present in actin bundles associated with contracting rings in spheroplasts.
source: Other components of actomyosin rings such as the regulatory light chain of myosin Rlc1p, tropomyosin Cdc8p (co-staining of these shown in Figure 2A), IQGAP protein Rng2p, and F-BAR protein Cdc15p (Figure 2A) were present in actin bundles associated with contracting rings in spheroplasts.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GFP-Rng2p, Cdc15p-GFP, and Rlc1p-GFP are associated with the expelling/expelled bundles.
source: We investigated the dynamics of ring contraction using each of these proteins as a marker and found that GFP-Rng2p, Cdc15p-GFP, and Rlc1p-GFP were associated with the expelling/expelled bundles (Figure 2B, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Video 2.

claim: Rlc1p-GFP is found in bundles associated with contracting rings in S. pombe.
source: In time-lapse imaging experiments, Rlc1p-GFP was also found in bundles associated with contracting rings in S. pombe (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data from S. pombe shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Actomyosin bundles become detectable when the ring contracts to a diameter of ~2 µm in spheroplasts of S. japonicus.
source: When the contracting ring was analyzed in spheroplasts of S. japonicus, actomyosin bundles became detectable when the ring contracted to a diameter of ~2 µm and were expelled from the ring at the rate of 2.19 ± 0.61 µm/min, (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Actomyosin bundles are expelled from the ring at the rate of 2.19 ± 0.61 µm/min in spheroplasts.
source: When the contracting ring was analyzed in spheroplasts of S. japonicus, actomyosin bundles became detectable when the ring contracted to a diameter of ~2 µm and were expelled from the ring at the rate of 2.19 ± 0.61 µm/min, (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between the number of actin bundles or bundle lengths with the perimeter of the actomyosin ring.
source: Profiling the distribution of ring-associated bundles in spheroplasts indicated that there was an inverse correlation (Figure 2Ei) between the number of actin bundles (measured using tropomyosin Cdc8p as a marker for actin bundles) or bundle lengths with the perimeter of the actomyosin ring (Figure 2Eii).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2Ei and 2Eii.

claim: There are on average 3.5 ± 1.8 actin bundles attached to rings of less than 11 µm perimeter.
source: It appeared that there were on average 3.5 ± 1.8 actin bundles attached to rings of less than 11 µm perimeter (corresponding to about 3.5 µm ring diameter), whereas there were 0.7 ± 1.2 actin bundles associated to rings of larger perimeter (Figure 2Eiii).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2Eiii.

claim: There are on average 0.7 ± 1.2 actin bundles associated to rings of larger than 11 µm perimeter.
source: It appeared that there were on average 3.5 ± 1.8 actin bundles attached to rings of less than 11 µm perimeter (corresponding to about 3.5 µm ring diameter), whereas there were 0.7 ± 1.2 actin bundles associated to rings of larger perimeter (Figure 2Eiii).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2Eiii.

claim: Individual actin bundles are longer in small rings (4.16 ± 3.30 µm for perimeter of <11 µm) than in larger rings (1.42 ± 1.86 µm for perimeter of >11 µm).
source: When the length of individual ring-associated actin bundles was measured, we found that on average the bundle was longer in small rings (4.16 ± 3.30 µm for perimeter of <11 µm) than in larger rings (1.42 ± 1.86 µm for perimeter of >11 µm) (Figure 2Eiv).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2Eiv.

claim: The total length of ring perimeters and actin bundles associated with the ring is higher in smaller rings compared to larger rings.
source: The total length of ring perimeters and actin bundles associated with the ring was higher in smaller rings compared to larger rings (Figure 2Ev).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2Ev.

claim: Ring disassembly and bundle expulsion is coupled to ring contraction.
source: These analyses indicated that ring disassembly and bundle expulsion was coupled to ring contraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between ring size and bundle characteristics.

claim: Ring-associated bundles become detectable after 12.3 ± 3.2 min of initiation of actomyosin ring contraction in mitotic cells.
source: On average, the ring-associated bundles became detectable after 12.3 ± 3.2 min of initiation of actomyosin ring contraction, and continued to be expelled from the actomyosin ring until the end of contraction at a rate of 1.91 ± 0.55 µm/min (Figure 2G; full contraction time was 18.21 ± 3.18 min).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Ring-associated bundles are expelled from the actomyosin ring at a rate of 1.91 ± 0.55 µm/min in mitotic cells.
source: On average, the ring-associated bundles became detectable after 12.3 ± 3.2 min of initiation of actomyosin ring contraction, and continued to be expelled from the actomyosin ring until the end of contraction at a rate of 1.91 ± 0.55 µm/min (Figure 2G; full contraction time was 18.21 ± 3.18 min).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Full contraction time of actomyosin rings in mitotic cells is 18.21 ± 3.18 min.
source: On average, the ring-associated bundles became detectable after 12.3 ± 3.2 min of initiation of actomyosin ring contraction, and continued to be expelled from the actomyosin ring until the end of contraction at a rate of 1.91 ± 0.55 µm/min (Figure 2G; full contraction time was 18.21 ± 3.18 min).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The expulsion of actomyosin bundles becomes obvious when rings contract to ~40% of the initial diameter.
source: Hence, it appeared that the expulsion of actomyosin bundles became obvious when rings contracted to ~40% of the initial diameter.
evidence: This is calculated from the ring diameter measurements (2.26 µm / 5.49 µm ≈ 40%).

claim: Treating S. japonicus cell ghosts with ATP induces contraction of isolated actomyosin rings.
source: Treating S. japonicus cell ghosts with ATP induced contraction of isolated actomyosin rings (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Actin bundles remain associated with the contracting and fully contracted rings in cell ghosts treated with ATP.
source: Interestingly, the actin bundles remained associated with the contracting and fully contracted rings (Figure 3B, Video 4) although the F-actin signal as visualized with LifeAct-GFP was lesser than in cells and spheroplasts.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and Video 4.

claim: Ring-associated bundles appearing in cell ghosts after ATP addition are similar to those observed during in vivo ring contraction.
source: The ring-associated bundles appearing in cell ghosts after ATP addition were similar to those observed during in vivo ring contraction (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on comparison with in vivo data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There are 4.3 ± 1.4 bundles associated with the rings in cell ghosts after ATP addition.
source: We observed 4.3 ± 1.4 bundles associated with the rings in cell ghosts, with individual average length of 3.9 ± 1.3 µm (Figure 3D; total bundle length 16.1 ± 6.7 µm).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Individual bundles in cell ghosts have an average length of 3.9 ± 1.3 µm.
source: We observed 4.3 ± 1.4 bundles associated with the rings in cell ghosts, with individual average length of 3.9 ± 1.3 µm (Figure 3D; total bundle length 16.1 ± 6.7 µm).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The sum F-actin intensity of cell ghosts (ring actin + bundle actin) following ATP addition shows no significant changes.
source: The sum F-actin intensity of cell ghosts (ring actin + bundle actin) following ATP addition showed no significant changes, whereas there was a decrease of actin intensity in the rings (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is a decrease of actin intensity in the rings of cell ghosts following ATP addition.
source: The sum F-actin intensity of cell ghosts (ring actin + bundle actin) following ATP addition showed no significant changes, whereas there was a decrease of actin intensity in the rings (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is no significant increase in the amount of actin and Cdc8p in the supernatant in cell ghosts treated with ATP for 20 or 40 min.
source: We did not find a significant increase in the amount of actin and Cdc8p in the supernatant in cell ghosts treated with ATP for 20 or 40 min (Figure 3F), consistent with the idea that ring contraction resulted in denser actin filaments containing binding proteins such as tropomyosin that remain in the pellet fraction.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Ring contraction results in denser actin filaments containing binding proteins such as tropomyosin that remain in the pellet fraction.
source: We did not find a significant increase in the amount of actin and Cdc8p in the supernatant in cell ghosts treated with ATP for 20 or 40 min (Figure 3F), consistent with the idea that ring contraction resulted in denser actin filaments containing binding proteins such as tropomyosin that remain in the pellet fraction.
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoblot data showing no increase in soluble proteins.

claim: Most actin is expelled in filaments contained in bundles during ring contraction in cell ghosts treated with ATP for 20 to 40 min.
source: These results indicated that in cell ghosts treated with ATP for 20 to 40 min, the rings reduced in actin amounts. However, this did not lead to an increase in soluble G-actin during ring contraction, suggesting that most actin was expelled in filaments contained in bundles during this period of time.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that actin is lost from rings but not found in the soluble fraction.

claim: The expulsion of actin bundles is a result of ring contraction and is independent of continuous presence of cytosol.
source: Furthermore, these experiments established that the expulsion of actin bundles was a result of ring contraction and was independent of continuous presence of cytosol.
evidence: This is concluded from the cell ghost experiments where cytosol is absent.

claim: The absence of cytosolic components such as G-actin suggests that the actomyosin bundles are expelled as a result of contraction rather than being newly polymerized actin cables.
source: Finally, the absence of cytosolic components such as G-actin also suggests that the actomyosin bundles are expelled as a result of contraction rather than the possibility that these bundles were newly polymerized actin cables that were not incorporated into the highly curved actomyosin ring (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from the cell ghost experiments lacking cytosolic components.

claim: The mean curvature at which bundles begin to be expelled is 1.1 ± 0.4 µm−1 in spheroplasts.
source: Although rings started with curvatures (1/radius) of even smaller than 0.4 µm−1 (translates to a ring diameter of >5 µm in spheroplasts), the mean curvature at which bundles began to be expelled was 1.1 ± 0.4 µm−1 (translates to a ring diameter of ~2 µm) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by curvature analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Bundle expulsion in rings is promoted by increased curvature.
source: Given that bundle expulsion was only observed after a significant reduction in ring diameter, suggesting that bundle expulsion in rings is promoted by increased curvature.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that bundles are expelled only at smaller ring diameters (higher curvatures).

claim: Approximately 68% of ring-associated bundles are detected at regions of increased local curvature in ATP treated cell ghosts.
source: Furthermore, even in partially contracted and curved actomyosin rings in ATP treated cell ghosts, the majority (~68%) of ring-associated bundles were detected at regions of increased local curvature where the ring appeared to be bent (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: About 95% of the actomyosin bundles are expelled from the curved regions of compressed rings compared to flat regions.
source: Strikingly, about 95% of the actomyosin bundles were expelled from the curved regions of compressed rings compared to flat regions (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 5; average 5.2 ± 0.9 bundles per ring), and the local curvature at the sites of expelled bundles was 1.5 ± 0.3 µm−1 (Figure 4E; mean curvature of compressed rings was 0.7 ± 0.2 µm−1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C, D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The local curvature at the sites of expelled bundles in compressed rings is 1.5 ± 0.3 µm−1.
source: Strikingly, about 95% of the actomyosin bundles were expelled from the curved regions of compressed rings compared to flat regions (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 5; average 5.2 ± 0.9 bundles per ring), and the local curvature at the sites of expelled bundles was 1.5 ± 0.3 µm−1 (Figure 4E; mean curvature of compressed rings was 0.7 ± 0.2 µm−1).
evidence: This is supported by curvature analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The mean curvature of compressed rings is 0.7 ± 0.2 µm−1.
source: Strikingly, about 95% of the actomyosin bundles were expelled from the curved regions of compressed rings compared to flat regions (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 5; average 5.2 ± 0.9 bundles per ring), and the local curvature at the sites of expelled bundles was 1.5 ± 0.3 µm−1 (Figure 4E; mean curvature of compressed rings was 0.7 ± 0.2 µm−1).
evidence: This is supported by curvature analysis data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Compressed rings have an average of 5.2 ± 0.9 bundles per ring.
source: Strikingly, about 95% of the actomyosin bundles were expelled from the curved regions of compressed rings compared to flat regions (Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Video 5; average 5.2 ± 0.9 bundles per ring), and the local curvature at the sites of expelled bundles was 1.5 ± 0.3 µm−1 (Figure 4E; mean curvature of compressed rings was 0.7 ± 0.2 µm−1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Actomyosin bundles are expelled when uncompressed rings contract to a perimeter of 6.3 ± 1.5 µm.
source: Whereas actomyosin bundles were expelled when uncompressed rings contracted to a perimeter of 6.3 ± 1.5 µm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), majority of compressed rings started releasing actomyosin bundles when contracted to a perimeter of only 12.5 ± 2.4 µm, indicating that the curvature change induced expulsion of actomyosin bundles (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Majority of compressed rings start releasing actomyosin bundles when contracted to a perimeter of 12.5 ± 2.4 µm.
source: Whereas actomyosin bundles were expelled when uncompressed rings contracted to a perimeter of 6.3 ± 1.5 µm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), majority of compressed rings started releasing actomyosin bundles when contracted to a perimeter of only 12.5 ± 2.4 µm, indicating that the curvature change induced expulsion of actomyosin bundles (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Curvature change induces expulsion of actomyosin bundles.
source: Whereas actomyosin bundles were expelled when uncompressed rings contracted to a perimeter of 6.3 ± 1.5 µm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), majority of compressed rings started releasing actomyosin bundles when contracted to a perimeter of only 12.5 ± 2.4 µm, indicating that the curvature change induced expulsion of actomyosin bundles (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of bundle expulsion in compressed vs. uncompressed rings.

claim: The ring contraction rate following compression is 0.37 ± 0.09 µm/min.
source: Curiously, following compression, the ring contraction rate (△perimeters/time) was 0.37 ± 0.09 µm/min, which was significantly less than the 1.26 ± 0.57 µm/min observed in uncompressed spheroplasts (Figure 4F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The ring contraction rate in uncompressed spheroplasts is 1.26 ± 0.57 µm/min.
source: Curiously, following compression, the ring contraction rate (△perimeters/time) was 0.37 ± 0.09 µm/min, which was significantly less than the 1.26 ± 0.57 µm/min observed in uncompressed spheroplasts (Figure 4F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bundles are expelled at a rate of 1.18 ± 0.42 µm/min in compressed spheroplasts.
source: The bundles were expelled at a reduced rate of 1.18 ± 0.42 µm/min as compared to 2.19 ± 0.61 µm/min in uncompressed spheroplasts (Figure 4G and Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Shortening of the flat regions (△d) of compressed rings occurs faster than the decrease of ring heights (△h).
source: Furthermore, shortening of the flat regions (△d) of compressed rings occurred faster than the decrease of ring heights (△h) (Figure 4H; △d/min= 0.16 ± 0.04 µm/min vs. △h/min = 0.07 ± 0.02 µm/min).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The actomyosin bundles are constrained by the local curvature of contracting rings.
source: Thus, the actomyosin bundles were constrained by the local curvature of contracting rings, and their expulsion depends on the curvature changes during ring contraction.
evidence: This is concluded from the compression experiments showing curvature-dependent bundle expulsion.

claim: Bundle expulsion depends on the curvature changes during ring contraction.
source: Thus, the actomyosin bundles were constrained by the local curvature of contracting rings, and their expulsion depends on the curvature changes during ring contraction.
evidence: This is concluded from the compression experiments showing curvature-dependent bundle expulsion.

claim: Ring disassembly is coupled physically to ring contraction in a ring-geometry coordinated manner.
source: Our results showed that ring disassembly is coupled physically to ring contraction in a ring-geometry coordinated manner.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the curvature-dependent bundle expulsion experiments.

claim: The expulsion of micron-scale actomyosin bundles may serve as a major mechanism to disassemble actomyosin rings during cytokinesis.
source: The expulsion of micron-scale actomyosin bundles may serve as a major mechanism to disassemble actomyosin rings during cytokinesis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: It is presently unclear if other mechanisms, such as cofilin and myosin II mediated filament severing/breakage and loss of actin monomers also contribute to actin disassembly during cytokinesis.
source: It is presently unclear if other mechanisms, such as cofilin and myosin II mediated filament severing / breakage and loss of actin monomers also contribute to actin disassembly during cytokinesis.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in current understanding.

claim: The coupling of bundle expulsion mediated-ring disassembly to ring contraction appears intrinsic to the ring itself.
source: The coupling of bundle expulsion mediated-ring disassembly to ring contraction appears intrinsic to the ring itself, and is potentially driven by a physical mechanism that is independent of cytosolic factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell ghost experiments showing bundle expulsion without cytosol.

claim: Bundle expulsion is potentially driven by a physical mechanism that is independent of cytosolic factors.
source: The coupling of bundle expulsion mediated-ring disassembly to ring contraction appears intrinsic to the ring itself, and is potentially driven by a physical mechanism that is independent of cytosolic factors.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell ghost experiments showing bundle expulsion without cytosol.

claim: It is possible that the affinity of binding of unidentified actin binding proteins with F-actin is reduced upon increased curvature of actin filaments.
source: It is possible that the affinity of binding of unidentified actin binding proteins with F-actin is reduced upon increased curvature of actin filaments.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observations.

claim: Attainment of a curved morphology is an energetically unfavorable conformation since actin filaments have a persistence length of ~10 microns.
source: It is likely that attainment of a curved morphology is an energetically unfavorable conformation since actin filaments have a persistence length of ~10 microns (which can increase further with bundling) (Ott et al., 1993; Riveline et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on known physical properties of actin filaments cited from prior work.

claim: Actin filament persistence length can increase further with bundling.
source: It is likely that attainment of a curved morphology is an energetically unfavorable conformation since actin filaments have a persistence length of ~10 microns (which can increase further with bundling) (Ott et al., 1993; Riveline et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on known physical properties of actin filaments cited from prior work.

claim: Other ring proteins do not associate tightly to actin bundles during ring contraction in a less crowded environment such as permeabilized cell ghosts.
source: It is possible that other ring proteins do not associate tightly to actin bundles during ring contraction in a less crowded environment (such as permeabilized cell ghosts), whereas they are able to associate with expelled bundles in a cellular environment of increased molecular crowding.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation that some proteins are not visible on bundles in cell ghosts.

claim: In the presence of cytosol, loss of ring proteins from actin bundles in the ring is balanced by replenishment from the cytosolic pool.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that, in the presence of cytosol, as in a cellular context (Pelham and Chang, 2002; Wong et al., 2002), loss of ring proteins from actin bundles in the ring is balanced by replenishment from the cytosolic pool.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation citing prior work on protein dynamics.

claim: In cell ghosts, replenishment of ring proteins does not occur due to the absence of cytosol.
source: However, in cell ghosts, such replenishment of ring proteins does not occur due to the absence of cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of the cell ghost system.

claim: Several types of actin filament behaviors such as branching and bundling are coupled to the curvature of the actin filament network.
source: Several types of actin filament behaviors such as branching and bundling are coupled to the curvature of the actin filament network (Liu et al., 2008; Risca et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Curvature-induced disassembly could be a general mechanism for disassembly of actomyosin networks.
source: Expulsion of the actomyosin bundles that occurs when the cytokinetic actomyosin ring acquires high curvature suggests that curvature-induced disassembly could be a general mechanism for disassembly of actomyosin networks.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other actomyosin systems.

claim: The STORM microscope has an axial resolution (x-y direction) of 22–28 nm.
source: The STORM microscope has been tested to have an axial resolution (x-y direction) of 22–28 nm, done as previously described (Nieuwenhuizen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a technical specification supported by citation.
